period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 7 periods = 280 minutes
Total: 7 periods · 4h 40min

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read (p.28): paired oral discussion — would experience differ without sight or hearing?
Let us read (p.28): paired recall of a visited place — senses chart.

time_bands.activity: Invite students to close their eyes briefly and identify classroom sounds and textures by touch. Use this quick paired exchange to surface the idea that senses shape how we know the world, bridging into Helen Keller's essay.

Read the essay aloud together, pages 28–31, with students following in their textbooks. Pause at the passage describing touch of the leaf and the silver birch bark to let students visualise and comment.

Pairs work on “Let us read” (p.28): each partner recalls a visited place and talks through what they saw, heard, smelt, tasted, and touched there. One partner records the five-sense details in their notebook.

Whole-class share: two or three pairs report — would the experience be different without sight or hearing? Teacher draws out that Keller knows the world richly through non-visual senses, setting up the essay’s central question.

periods.teacher_notes: Keller’s essay opens by establishing touch as a rich sense before arguing for sight’s supremacy; students sometimes flatten this to ‘blind people are sad’ — draw out wonder and compensatory richness instead. The pre-reading sensory recall (p.28) is the bridge into that nuance. Task on imagining life without sight (p.28, oral) is not anchored today; flag it as a reflective journal prompt for self-study.

periods.activity_title: Three Days Mapped: Comprehension and Close Reading

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.31): identify four true statements about Keller’s wishes and values.
Let us discuss (p.32): complete three-day table with Keller’s planned activities.
Let us discuss (p.32): how does Keller understand feelings without sight — ‘window of the soul’.

time_bands.activity: Continue reading the essay aloud, pages 31–33, with students following. This unhurried reading aloud covers the three-day vision plan and the closing advocacy passage.
Students work individually on “Let us discuss I” (p.31): read the seven statements and mark which four are true. Pairs compare answers before whole-class verification with the teacher.

Whole class builds the three-day table together on the board (“Let us discuss II”, p.32): teacher elicits Day 1 (people who enriched her life), Day 2 (dawn and museums), Day 3 (city corner, human faces), and students copy the completed table.

Discuss “Let us discuss III” (p.32): how does Keller understand people’s feelings without seeing their eyes? Students share evidence from the text (feel of faces, broad emotions) and the teacher draws out the ‘window of the soul’ metaphor.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often confuse Day 2’s museum visit with a leisure trip; clarify that Keller frames it as witnessing the condensed pageant of human progress, connecting to her broader argument about the value of sight. The true/false set (p.31) surfaces two common misreadings — that she values only suffering and that touch brings the greatest joy — address both directly. Extract-analysis tasks (p.32–33) are not anchored today; they are self-study reading exercises students can attempt independently.
materials: Blackboard or whiteboard for three-day table

periods.activity_title: Reflecting Deeply: Inference and Critical Response

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.33): why does Keller believe sight is the most wonderful sense?
Let us think and reflect (p.33): what do her three-day choices reveal about her values and priorities?

homework.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.33): write a paragraph — how might Keller’s view guide kinder attitudes toward people with special abilities?

time_bands.activity: Re-read together the closing paragraphs of the essay (p.33) where Keller appeals to sighted readers to use their eyes as if tomorrow they might be blind. Students underline the key imperative phrases.

Whole-class discussion: why does Keller call sight ‘the most delightful’ sense (“Let us think and reflect II”, p.33)? Students cite specific evidence from the essay; teacher charts responses under ‘what touch can do’ and ‘what only sight can do’.

Independent written response to “Let us think and reflect II” (p.33): what do Keller’s three-day choices — people, history, living humanity — tell us about her values? Students draft in notebooks; two volunteers share, and teacher provides oral formative feedback.

periods.teacher_notes: The essay’s closing appeal to sighted readers is the pivot from personal longing to universal advocacy; students who focus only on the three days miss this shift — draw it out explicitly. The question about values (p.33) rewards textual evidence about Keller’s emphasis on human connection over scenic beauty or material experience. The extended-response items on significance of imagining sense-loss and on everyday sensory engagement (p.33) are not anchored in class; point students to them as self-study reflection prompts.

periods.activity_title: Listening to Inclusion, Speaking About Senses

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.36): identify four true statements from the mother-and-son Braille and Digital India conversation.
Let us speak (p.36): one-minute paired talk on the sense each student values most, using the given prompts.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the listening task: students will hear a conversation between Anuj and his mother about a new classmate, Braille, and the Digital India initiative. Ask students to read the seven statements (p.36) silently before listening begins.

Read the conversation transcript aloud at natural pace (“Let us listen”, p.36). Students mark which four statements they believe are true. Read it a second time; students confirm or revise their choices, then pairs compare before whole-class check.

Introduce the speaking task (“Let us speak”, p.36): display the prompt frame on the board. Give pairs a moment to choose their sense and mentally frame their response using the prompts before speaking begins.

Pairs take turns: each partner speaks for approximately a minute on the sense they value most. Teacher circulates, offering brief encouragement. Three or four volunteers share with the class; teacher comments on fluency and use of the prompt structure.

periods.teacher_notes: The listening text connects Keller’s personal experience of visual impairment to a contemporary inclusive-education context; help students see this bridge. A common error in the true/false set is selecting statement 5 (Anuj already knew visually impaired people can use computers) — the transcript clearly shows he is surprised, so address this misconception directly. Encourage hesitant speakers by pointing out that all five sense-prompts are equally valid and personal.

periods.activity_title: Writing a Descriptive Paragraph: Sense by Sense

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.37): plan, draft, and revise a three-part descriptive paragraph about a recently visited place.

time_bands.activity: Read the model guidelines for descriptive writing (“Let us write”, p.37) together. Teacher explains the three-part structure — attention-grabbing opening, sensory supporting lines, final impression — and briefly illustrates each part on the board using Keller’s essay as a mentor text.

Students plan their paragraph: they jot down their chosen place, three to five sensory details across sight, sound, smell, taste, and touch, and a closing impression. Teacher circulates and prompts those who are stuck with open questions about their chosen place.
Students draft their descriptive paragraph independently, aiming to include at least one alliteration, simile, or personification in the supporting lines as instructed on p.37.

Peer response: partners exchange drafts and check for the three-part structure and at least one literary device. Two volunteers read their paragraphs aloud; class offers one strength and one suggestion. Teacher provides brief oral formative feedback on language choices.

periods.teacher_notes: Keller’s essay models exactly the sensory detail this task demands — refer students back to her descriptions of the silver birch bark and the quivering bird as examples of touch and sound rendered precisely. Students often write only visual details; the planning step is where to intervene and prompt the other four senses. Drafting, peer response, and revision all happen within this sitting so the paragraph is complete by the end.

periods.activity_title: Sensory Words and Modal Verbs in Context

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.34): complete the five-sense sensory word table from the essay text and add new words.
Let us learn (p.34): identify modal verbs in five sentences and match each to its function.
Let us learn (p.35): fill in blanks with appropriate modal verbs for seven function-labelled situations.

time_bands.activity: Introduce sensory vocabulary (“Let us learn I”, p.34): students scan the essay to find words for each sense and complete Column 2 of the table; they then brainstorm new words for Column 3 in pairs. Class builds a composite table on the board.

Introduce modal verbs (“Let us learn II”, p.34): teacher reads each sentence aloud, students underline the modal verb, then match it to its function (possibility, necessity, polite request, ability, moral obligation) from the box. Discuss each answer with the class, drawing examples from Keller’s repeated use of ‘should’ in the essay.

Students complete the modal verb fill-in-the-blank task (“Let us learn IV”, p.35) individually. Pairs swap notebooks to check; volunteers explain the function of their chosen modal to the class. Teacher addresses common confusions between ‘can’ and ‘may’ for permission.

periods.teacher_notes: Keller’s essay itself is rich in modal verbs — particularly her repeated ‘should’ when describing her imagined three days — and students should see these drawn from the text before tackling decontextualised sentences. Sensory words from Column 2 (panorama, relish, rough) are already in the textbook table; students may need prompting to look beyond the listed examples when adding Column 3 words.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore (p.37–38): study the Braille code and write one’s own name using bindis or daal grains.
Let us explore (p.38): research and write findings about the International Day of Persons with Disabilities in India.

homework.task_brief: Let us explore (p.38): visit the NCERT Indian Sign Language link and learn five signs to share with the class.

time_bands.activity: Briefly recall Keller’s description of reading by touch and introduce the Braille system (“Let us explore I”, p.37–38). Distribute bindis or small lentil grains if available; students will use these to form Braille dots.

Students study the Braille code chart in the textbook (p.37–38) and spell out their own name using the dot pattern, pressing bindis or grains onto paper. Pairs check each other’s Braille names. Teacher circulates, drawing attention to the tactile reading experience Keller describes.

Students draft a short write-up (“Let us explore II”, p.38) on the International Day of Persons with Disabilities: when it falls, how India observes it, and one inclusion initiative they find significant. They use prior knowledge and any classroom reference materials available.

Two or three students read their write-ups aloud. Teacher collects the sheets to display on the class board as directed on p.38, and sets the Indian Sign Language link (p.38) as a home exploration task.

periods.teacher_notes: The Braille activity gives students a tactile echo of Keller’s world and should feel exploratory rather than assessed; celebrate effort and curiosity over accuracy. For the Disabilities Day write-up, students may not have researched beforehand — accept reasonable prior knowledge and clarify any factual gaps on the board (3 December, UNCRPD). The Indian Sign Language task (p.38) is assigned as homework because it requires internet access not available in class.

items.source_lo: Student identifies explicit and implicit information in an informational essay using comprehension and critical reading as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Helen Keller’s three-day vision plan, the ‘window of the soul’ metaphor, and her advocacy for mindful sensory engagement.
items.item_stem:
Read the statements below about Helen Keller’s imagined three days of sight. Write True or False for each statement.
1. On the first day, Keller would visit museums to see the history of human progress.
2. Keller states that she would spend the first day seeing the faces of the people whose kindness had enriched her life.
3. On the third day, Keller plans to stand at a busy city corner and watch ordinary people going about their lives.
4. Keller concludes that touch is the most delightful of all the senses.

options.text: Keller concludes that touch is the most delightful of all the senses.
Keller states that she would spend the first day seeing the faces of the people whose kindness had enriched her life.
On the first day, Keller would visit museums to see the history of human progress.
On the third day, Keller plans to stand at a busy city corner and watch ordinary people going about their lives.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. False — the museum visit belongs to the second day, not the first. 2. True — Keller explicitly reserves Day 1 for the people who have shaped her life. 3. True — the third day is devoted to watching humanity at a city corner. 4. False — Keller concludes that sight must be the most delightful sense.

items.source_lo: Student identifies explicit and implicit information in an informational essay using comprehension and critical reading as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Helen Keller’s three-day vision plan, the ‘window of the soul’ metaphor, and her advocacy for mindful sensory engagement.
items.item_stem: In her essay, Helen Keller calls the eye the “window of the soul” and admits that, without sight, she can feel broad emotions on a person’s face but not the subtleties the eye communicates. She closes by urging sighted readers to use their eyes as if they might lose sight tomorrow. What does this appeal reveal about Keller’s central purpose in the essay? Support your answer with at least one detail from the text.

expected_elements: Identifies Keller’s purpose as urging mindful, grateful use of sight.
References the ‘window of the soul’ metaphor or the closing appeal.
Connects her personal deprivation to a universal lesson for sighted people.
Uses at least one phrase or detail drawn from the essay.

items.source_lo: Student listens critically to a conversation and selects information that is explicitly supported, using listen-and-respond as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Anuj and his mother discussing Braille, Digital India, screen readers, and inclusion mindset for visually impaired persons.
items.item_stem:
Listen to the conversation between Anuj and his mother. Then answer: According to Anuj’s mother, what does Digital India do for visually impaired people? Choose the correct answer.
A. It provides free Braille textbooks to all visually impaired students.
B. It offers assistive technologies such as screen readers and voice-enabled smartphones.
C. It trains visually impaired people to become computer programmers.
D. It builds special schools for students with visual impairments.

options.label: A
options.text: It builds special schools for students with visual impairments.

options.label: B
options.text: It offers assistive technologies such as screen readers and voice-enabled smartphones.

options.label: C
options.text: It provides free Braille textbooks to all visually impaired students.

options.label: D
options.text: It trains visually impaired people to become computer programmers.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Confuses Braille (mentioned in relation to Tara’s writing) with a Digital India service not stated in the conversation.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Overstates the scope of Digital India; the mother mentions IT as a field opened up, not a training programme.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Conflates inclusion infrastructure with physical schools, a detail absent from the transcript.

items.source_lo: Student listens critically to a conversation and selects information that is explicitly supported, using listen-and-respond as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Anuj and his mother discussing Braille, Digital India, screen readers, and inclusion mindset for visually impaired persons.
items.item_stem: Anuj’s mother ends the conversation by saying, “Inclusion is not just about having the right tools, but also the right mindset.” Based on the conversation you listened to, explain in one or two sentences what she means by ‘the right mindset’ and why she considers it as important as the tools.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The right mindset means genuinely accepting and valuing people with disabilities as independent, capable individuals — not just tolerating them. Anuj’s mother implies that technology alone cannot create inclusion if the people around a person with a disability do not hold respectful, open attitudes.

items.source_context: Speaking for one minute about the sense each student values most, using structured prompts about experience and loss.
items.item_stem: Think of the sense you value the most — sight, hearing, touch, smell, or taste. Describe one specific experience in your life when that sense gave you joy or helped you. Speak clearly for about one minute.

expected_elements: Names the chosen sense clearly at the start.
Describes a specific personal experience linked to that sense.
Uses at least two vivid describing words.
Speaks in complete sentences with reasonable fluency.

items.source_lo: Student expresses a personal view fluently with supporting reasons, using guided oral presentation as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Speaking for one minute about the sense each student values most, using structured prompts about experience and loss.
items.item_stem: Helen Keller believed that people who can see take their sight for granted. Do you agree or disagree? Give at least two reasons for your opinion, drawing on what you know from daily life or from Keller’s essay. Speak for about one minute.

expected_elements: States a clear agree or disagree position at the outset.
Gives two distinct reasons with brief supporting examples.
References Keller’s argument or a detail from the essay.
Maintains a coherent line of thought throughout.

items.source_lo: Student constructs a well-structured descriptive paragraph using sensory details and literary devices, using guided writing as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Three-part descriptive paragraph about a visited place: attention-grabbing opening, five-sense supporting lines with alliteration, simile or personification, closing impression.
items.item_stem: Write a descriptive paragraph about a park, market, or any outdoor place you have visited. Begin with one interesting sentence that captures the reader’s attention, then describe the place using details from at least three of your five senses. End with a sentence that gives a final impression of the place. Your paragraph should be seven to ten sentences long.

expected_elements: Opens with a striking sentence that names the place.
Includes sensory details from at least three different senses.
Uses at least one alliteration, simile, or personification.
Closes with a sentence capturing the overall impression.

items.source_lo: Student constructs a well-structured descriptive paragraph using sensory details and literary devices, using guided writing as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Three-part descriptive paragraph about a visited place: attention-grabbing opening, five-sense supporting lines with alliteration, simile or personification, closing impression.
items.item_stem: Imagine you are Helen Keller and you have been given three days of sight. Write a descriptive paragraph about the very first thing you would choose to see. Use vivid sensory details and at least one literary device — a simile, personification, or alliteration — to bring your description to life. Your paragraph should be eight to twelve sentences long.

expected_elements: Adopts Keller’s perspective convincingly throughout the paragraph.
Uses vivid, specific sensory details beyond sight alone.
Includes at least one identified literary device used effectively.
Sustains imaginative engagement with a coherent emotional tone.

items.item_stem: Match each sensory word from Helen Keller’s essay in Column A with the sense it primarily appeals to in Column B.
items.visual_stimulus:
Column A (Word from the essay)|Column B (Sense it appeals to)
panorama|touch
relish|sight
rough|taste
music|smell
perfume|hearing

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: panorama – sight; relish – taste; rough – touch; music – hearing; perfume – smell

items.source_lo: Student identifies and applies sensory vocabulary and modal verbs in context, using linguistic analysis of the essay as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Sensory words (panorama, relish, rough) mapped to five senses; modal verbs (should, can, must, may, ought to) and their functions in the essay.
items.item_stem: Helen Keller uses the modal verb ‘should’ repeatedly when describing her imagined three days — for example, “I should arise with the dawn” and “I should go to the museums.” Write two sentences of your own about something you would ideally like to do this week, using two different modal verbs (for example, should, must, can, may, or ought to). After each sentence, write in brackets the function the modal verb expresses (possibility, necessity, advice, ability, or polite request).

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Answers will vary. A correct response uses two different modal verbs, each in a grammatically complete sentence, with the function labelled accurately in brackets — for example: “I should visit the library more often. [advice]” and “I must finish my project before the deadline. [necessity].”

items.source_context: Braille code exploration by writing one’s name with tactile materials; International Day of Persons with Disabilities observation in India.
items.item_stem: Using the Braille code chart in your textbook, spell out the word LIGHT in Braille by drawing the correct dot pattern for each letter in the boxes below. Then write one sentence explaining why this activity gives you a better understanding of how Helen Keller experienced the world through touch.

expected_elements: Draws recognisably correct Braille dot patterns for L, I, G, H, T.
Sentence connects the tactile act to Keller’s experience meaningfully.
Shows awareness that Braille substitutes touch for visual reading.
Writing is clear and in complete sentences.

items.source_lo: Student extends understanding of disability inclusion through hands-on investigation and research, using interdisciplinary project work as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Braille code exploration by writing one’s name with tactile materials; International Day of Persons with Disabilities observation in India.
items.item_stem: The International Day of Persons with Disabilities is observed globally each year. Find out: (a) the date on which it is observed, (b) the theme or focus India adopted in a recent year, and (c) one specific initiative or event through which it is marked in Indian schools or communities. Present your findings as a short illustrated write-up (one paragraph with a title) that could be displayed on a class notice board.

expected_elements: Correctly states 3 December as the date of observance.
Mentions a specific recent theme or Indian government initiative.
Describes one school or community activity linked to the day.
Write-up has a clear title and is suitable for a notice board.
